client: I lost my grandmother about a month ago, and honestly, I've been struggling more than I expected. I can't seem to focus on anything — work, errands, even just making meals feels like this huge effort. I'm not sure talking about it is really going to change anything, but I figured I should at least try something because I can't keep going like this.
therapist:
It takes real courage to reach out even when part of you isn't sure it will help, and I want you to know that what you're feeling — that heaviness, the difficulty with even the smallest tasks — is a completely natural response to losing someone you loved. Grief has a way of quietly taking up so much of our energy that ordinary life can start to feel almost impossible, and that doesn't mean something is wrong with you. 

I'm wondering, when you think about your grandmother, what feeling tends to come up most strongly for you?

client: When I think about her, the first thing that hits me is this wave of guilt, honestly. Like, I keep going back to the last few months before she passed, thinking about all the times I was too busy or too tired to call her back, and I just... I can't seem to let that go. It's almost worse than the sadness itself, because at least the sadness feels like it makes sense, but the guilt just makes me feel like a terrible person.
therapist:
That guilt sounds absolutely exhausting to carry, and I really hear how much it's weighing on you — but I also want to gently reflect something back to you: the very fact that you're feeling this so deeply speaks to how much you loved her, not to what kind of person you are. It's worth asking whether you're holding yourself to a standard of perfection that you probably wouldn't apply to someone else you care about in the same situation.

If a close friend told you they'd been too busy or tired to call their grandmother back sometimes, would you truly see them as a terrible person?

client: I hear what you're saying, and no, I wouldn't judge a friend that harshly... but it still feels different when it's me. Like, I know logically that I was busy and tired, but she's gone now and I can't fix it, so the logic doesn't really reach the guilt, if that makes sense. It's like there's this wall between my head and my chest, and the reasonable thoughts just bounce off.
therapist:
What you just described — that wall between your head and your chest — is such a vivid and honest way to put it, and it makes complete sense, because grief and guilt live in a different place than logic does, and you can't simply think your way through them. What often helps is less about convincing yourself of the "right" answer and more about gently sitting with those feelings and slowly building a bridge between that reasonable part of you and the hurting part.

I'm curious — are there any memories of your grandmother where you *did* show up for her, moments where you felt genuinely connected, that your mind tends to skip over when the guilt takes hold?

client: There are a few memories, yeah... like when I used to call her on Sunday mornings and she'd talk for an hour about her garden, and I'd actually just sit there and listen, not rushing her off the phone. But my brain kind of... dismisses those, like they don't count because they weren't there at the end when it actually mattered. I guess I'm worried that if I let myself hold onto those good memories, I'm somehow letting myself off the hook too easily.
therapist:
There's something really important in what you just said — your mind has quietly set up a rule that the good memories "don't count," while the painful ones carry all the weight, and that's actually a very common pattern in grief that ends up being incredibly unfair to you. Those Sunday morning calls *were* her end, in the sense that they were the fabric of your relationship, the real and loving thing you built together over years.

I'd gently challenge the idea that honoring those memories means letting yourself "off the hook" — what if holding onto them isn't about excusing anything, but about seeing the full, true picture of who you were to her?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe it, but it feels almost too easy, like I'm just looking for permission to feel less guilty. Those Sunday calls were real, I know that, but they also feel distant now, like they belong to a different version of me and her. I guess what scares me is that if I start leaning into those good memories, the guilt might just be waiting underneath, ready to remind me that I wasn't there when it actually mattered.
therapist:
That fear makes so much sense — it's like the guilt has become a kind of guard, and part of you worries that lowering it means being ambushed by something even more painful underneath. But I want to sit with something you said: you're not looking for permission to *stop* caring, you're looking for permission to grieve someone you genuinely loved, and those are very different things.

What do you think your grandmother, knowing you the way she did, would want you to carry forward from your time together?

client: I've thought about that question before, and honestly, I think she'd want me to remember the good stuff — the way she'd laugh at her own jokes before she even finished telling them, or how she always made me feel like I wasn't too much for anyone. But then I immediately feel like I'm just telling myself a nice story to make the guilt go away, like I'm using her to let myself off the hook. It's hard to trust that answer when part of me keeps saying I don't deserve to feel comforted by it.
therapist:
The part of you that says you don't deserve comfort — that's worth paying close attention to, because that's a really painful belief to be carrying, and it may be doing more harm than the guilt itself. Your grandmother sounds like someone who made you feel like you weren't "too much," and there's something quietly heartbreaking about the idea that her love for you is one of the few things you're not allowing yourself to receive right now.

I'm wondering — where do you think that belief comes from, the one that says you don't deserve to be comforted?

client: I think it comes from a long time of feeling like I was too much for people — too emotional, too needy, too sensitive. Like at some point I just internalized that if I needed comfort, I was burdening whoever I asked it from. And honestly, hearing you say that my grandmother's love is something I'm not letting myself receive right now... that hit harder than I expected, because I think you're right and I don't really know what to do with that.
therapist:
That moment of recognition you just had — sitting with that rather than rushing past it — is actually really significant, and I want you to know it's okay not to know what to do with it yet. What you're describing, this long-held belief that your needs make you a burden, sounds like something that's been quietly shaping how you move through the world long before you lost your grandmother.

I'm gently curious — when you imagine actually letting yourself receive her love and those good memories, even just for a moment, what comes up in your body?

client: When I try to imagine that... letting her love just in, without immediately feeling like I didn't deserve it... there's this tightness in my chest, like something wants to open but also wants to stay shut. It's almost easier to focus on the grief than to sit with the warmth, because the warmth feels fragile somehow, like if I let myself really feel it, I'll lose it all over again. I don't know if that makes any sense.
therapist:
It makes complete sense, and what you just described is actually a profound insight — that the warmth feels dangerous because it carries the risk of loss, so grief becomes almost safer to hold onto than love. That fragility you're feeling isn't a sign that the warmth isn't real; it's a sign of how much she meant to you, and how tenderly you're trying to protect something precious.

I want to ask you gently — what might it look like to let that warmth in just a little at a time, not all at once, but in small enough doses that it feels less like something that could overwhelm you?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe that's possible... but I honestly don't know how to do that in small doses. It's like the warmth and the grief are all tangled up together, and I'm afraid that if I let one in, the other just floods in right behind it. How do you actually control something like that?
therapist:
The honest answer is that you don't fully control it — and that's actually okay, because the goal isn't to manage grief like a faucet but to slowly build your capacity to be with it without it sweeping you away completely. One small, concrete place to start might be allowing yourself just one of those Sunday morning memories — her laughing at her own jokes — for a brief moment, and then gently noticing what's there without needing to fix or push away whatever comes up.

What would it feel like to try something like that, even just as a small experiment, knowing you could put it down again whenever you needed to?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to try it, but honestly the idea of intentionally opening that door even a little bit feels terrifying. Like, what if I let myself think about her laughing and then I just... can't stop, and it turns into this whole spiral that ruins the rest of my day? I guess I'm not sure I trust myself to "put it down again" like you're describing.
therapist:
That fear of losing control is so understandable, and it tells me something important — that right now you need to build a little more safety and trust in yourself before stepping toward those memories, and that's not avoidance, that's wisdom. We don't have to open any doors today; what matters is that you're already doing something really hard just by being here and saying all of this out loud.

I'm wondering — are there small things that already help you feel grounded or settled when life feels overwhelming, even little things like a cup of tea or a certain place you like to sit?
